entries.text: A Dataset whose value arrives over HTTP — a reactive remote resource. The one thing to know: fetch() is explicit — a DataSource does not auto-load (auto = true is a deliberate opt-in for reactive addresses, not the default). Call it when the data should load (typically onInit, or on a user action); value and status then settle together, a frame ahead, so a constraint reading .loaded and one reading .value never disagree. Read the lifecycle through bindings — .loading, .loaded, .failed, .value, .error — none are settable attributes; clear() returns it to idle. The response is parsed JSON by default; format = "text" fetches textual material instead — a Markdown article, a source file — as one string (see format). weather: DataSource [ url = { /api/weather?zip=${zip} } ], onInit() { this.weather.fetch() }, // nothing loads until you ask report: View [ visible = { weather.loaded }, datapath = { weather.value?.rss?.channel } ] // :paths below read the response

entries.title: DataSource.url
entries.text: The resource URL — a literal or a { } constraint, so the source re-points reactively: change a dependency (a zip, a filter) and the next fetch() hits the new URL. Setting url does not load on its own — fetching stays explicit unless you opt into auto. string

entries.title: DataSource.format
entries.text: What the fetched bytes are: "json" (the default) parses the response and tags it for :path navigation; "text" delivers the raw bytes as one string in .value. Text is a first-class material, not a detail — it is how an authored Markdown file is loaded directly, with no JSON wrapping beside it: consume it whole, text = { article.value "" }. A string has nothing to navigate into, so the structural machinery — datapath, :path, schema, <-> — does not apply to a text source; the lifecycle (fetch(), .loading, .loaded, .failed) is identical. Loaded text renders clean through Markdown: HTML comments in the file are annotation, and annotation never renders. article: DataSource [ url = "guide.md", format = "text" ], doc: Markdown [ visible = { article.loaded }, text = { article.value "" } ] string

entries.title: DataSource.method
entries.text: The HTTP verb — "GET" by default. A body-carrying verb ("POST", "PUT", "PATCH") sends body with the request. A DataSource stays a source either way: the response lands in value and the status flags exactly as a GET's would, so a POST that returns the created record leaves you reading it like anything else. string

entries.title: DataSource.body
entries.text: The payload for a non-GET method — an object or array (JSON-encoded on the way out), or a string (sent as-is). Ignored on a GET. Like url it can be a { } constraint, so the payload re-derives from live state; also like url, changing it sends nothing until the next fetch(). object

entries.title: DataSource.auto
entries.text: Fetch unprompted whenever url arrives or changes, instead of waiting for fetch(). Off by default, and the default is the discipline — explicit loading is what stops a source firing requests nobody asked for as unrelated dependencies settle. Turn it on when the address is the reactive thing: a detail pane whose url derives from the current selection, where "the URL changed" and "load it" are the same event. With auto off, changing url arms the next fetch() and does nothing else. detail: DataSource [ auto = true, url = { "/api/issue/" + app.selectedId } ] boolean

entries.title: DataSource.credentials
entries.text: How to handle cookies, TLS client certificates, and authentication headers — the Fetch API's three modes, spelled as tokens. sameOrigin — the default, send only when url shares the page's origin omit — never send credentials or cookies with the request include — send cross-origin too, so an app can carry a session cookie/header/cert to a separately-hosted authenticated API. This only takes effect if that origin's CORS response allows credentials explicitly — a wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin: cannot combine with it; the response must echo back the specific requesting origin instead. sameOrigin is the camelCase spelling of the wire's same-origin (a hyphen is subtraction, so it cannot be a token) — the same translation blend makes for CSS's color-dodge. Since url may be a { } constraint, include sends credentials wherever that expression resolves: keep the address under your own control. notes: DataSource [ url = "https://api.example.com/notes", credentials = include ] omit | sameOrigin | include

entries.title: DataSource.status
entries.text: The lifecycle as one fact: "idle" before anything is asked, "loading" in flight, then "loaded" or "failed". Read-only — fetch() and clear() move it. The four booleans below derive from it, so they can never disagree with it or with each other. idle | loading | loaded | failed

entries.title: DataSource.idle
entries.text: Nothing has been asked for yet, or clear() returned it here. = { status == "idle" }. boolean

entries.title: DataSource.loading
entries.text: A request is in flight. = { status == "loading" } — the slot to hang a spinner on. boolean

entries.title: DataSource.loaded
entries.text: The latest fetch finished and validated. = { status == "loaded" }. It is about the request, not the value: a refetch (a changed url under auto, or fetch() again) drops it to false until the new response lands, while value still holds the previous one. So visible = { data.loaded } blinks on every refresh; a screen that should stay put while data refreshes guards on presence instead — visible = { data.value != null } — and keeps loaded/loading for what they name, the request's state. boolean

entries.title: DataSource.failed
entries.text: The request, or the schema check, refused. = { status == "failed" }. Read error for the one-line reason, statusCode and errorBody for what the server actually said. boolean

entries.title: DataSource.error
entries.text: Why the last fetch failed, as one line — an HTTP status, a transport message, or the schema mismatch with its pointed path. null when nothing has gone wrong. It is the message; the server's own account is errorBody. string

entries.title: DataSource.statusCode
entries.text: The HTTP status of the last reply — 404, 422, 200. 0 means no reply arrived: nothing asked yet, or the request never reached a server at all. That distinction is the point of the slot, since it separates "retry" from "report" without parsing error. number

entries.title: DataSource.errorBody
entries.text: What the server said when it refused — parsed if it was JSON, the raw text otherwise, null if the body was empty. This is the part that names which field failed or when the rate limit resets; a refusal reported as a status number alone throws it away. value is untouched by a failure, so the last good data is still there. object

entries.title: DataSource.fetch
entries.text: Loads (or reloads) the resource from the current url, then settles value and the status flags together, a frame ahead. Loading is a verb you call, not something that happens to you, so you decide when (usually in onInit, or on a user action). Calling it again re-fetches; change url's dependencies first to fetch a new address. Returns a Promise you can await, but the reactive flags are the idiomatic path. fetch(): Promise<void>

entries.title: DataSource.clear
entries.text: Returns the source to the idle state — drops value, error, and the loaded/failed flags, as if it had never fetched. For resetting a search field's results, or releasing a large response you no longer need. clear(): void

entries.title: DataSource.load
entries.text: Fires when a fetch settles successfully, after value and the flags are consistent — a handler reading value sees the arrived data, never the previous one. Failures do not fire it; they set failed and error. You usually do not need this: any binding reading .value or a :path beneath it already updates on arrival, which is the entire reactive point. Reach for onLoad only when arrival must cause something a binding cannot express — focusing the first result, chaining a follow-up fetch, announcing to a screen reader. onLoad()

entries.title: Animator
entries.text: Drives one numeric attribute from from to to over duration, on a motion curve — the timed half of the animation family. A non-visual node you place inside the view it animates, naming the target slot with attribute. For motion toward a live, reactive target (one that keeps moving), reach for Spring instead — an Animator runs a fixed from→to and stops. box: View [ opacity = 0, fadeIn: Animator [ attribute = opacity, to = 1, duration = 300, started = true ] ]

entries.title: Animator.attribute
entries.text: The target slot this animator drives — a bare attribute name of the enclosing view (attribute = opacity), checked to be numeric. Not a string, not a path; the raw slot reference. slot

entries.title: Animator.to
entries.text: The value to animate to. number

entries.title: Animator.from
entries.text: The value to start from — omit it to sample the target's current value at start, so an animation begins wherever the view already is (the usual case). number

entries.title: Animator.duration
entries.text: The run time, in ms. number

entries.title: Animator.repeat
entries.text: How many times to repeat; 0/absent runs once. number

entries.title: Animator.motion
entries.text: The easing curve — a motion token (quad, back, …) naming the shape of the interpolation between from and to. Motion

entries.title: Animator.relative
entries.text: When true, to/from are offsets from the current value rather than absolute targets — "move by", not "move to". boolean

entries.title: Animator.started
entries.text: Set true to run it — the declarative start(). Drive it from a constraint to gate playback on state: every change drives the run — true starts, false stops in place, and a fresh true is a fresh run from the top. started is the request, not a status readback: a run that completes (or is stop()ed) leaves it reading whatever was asked, so ask atRest or onStop for arrival, never started. boolean

entries.title: Animator.paused
entries.text: Freeze a running animation and resume it without resetting — distinct from started, which runs it from the top. A paused animation costs nothing: it holds no frame loop, and resuming continues from the freeze as if no time had passed. boolean

entries.title: Animator.atRest
entries.text: Read-only. Motion at rest, as a reactive fact: true only at an uninterrupted destination — the animation twin of a DataSource's .loaded. The animator computes it; start() and stop() are what move it. Read it to sequence what should happen after motion (revealing a detail panel once its container has finished opening) instead of guessing with a timer that a retarget would invalidate. (Not to be confused with the settle , the update transaction — a spring comes to rest across many settles.) boolean

entries.title: Animator.start
entries.text: Runs the animation from the current attribute value toward to — the imperative trigger, equivalent to setting started = true. Prefer binding started to a condition when the run is state-driven; call start() for a one-shot fired from a handler (onClick() { fx.start() }). start(): void

entries.title: Animator.stop
entries.text: Halts the run where it is and leaves the attribute at its current value — it does not snap back to from. Pair with start() for handler-driven control, or drive started reactively instead. stop(): void

entries.title: Animator.start
entries.text: Fires when the run begins (answered by onStart). onStart()

entries.title: Animator.stop
entries.text: Fires when the run ends (answered by onStop) — the hook for chaining or cleanup. onStop()

entries.title: Animator.repeat
entries.text: Fires at each loop of a repeating run (answered by onRepeat). onRepeat()

entries.title: AnimatorGroup
entries.text: Coordinates several Animators as a unit, running them sequential (one after another, the default) or simultaneous (all at once). Its own to / from / duration / motion / attribute / relative / repeat are a default cascade — a member that omits one inherits the group's — so shared timing is written once, on the group. reveal: AnimatorGroup [ process = sequential, duration = 200, Animator [ attribute = opacity, to = 1 ], Animator [ attribute = y, to = 0 ] ]

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.attribute
entries.text: A default target slot cascaded to any member that omits its own (see Animator.attribute). slot

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.to
entries.text: The default destination, inherited by members that omit to. number

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.from
entries.text: The default start value, inherited by members that omit from. number

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.duration
entries.text: The default run time (ms), inherited by members that omit duration — the usual way to give a whole group one tempo. number

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.repeat
entries.text: The default repeat count for members that omit repeat. number

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.motion
entries.text: The default easing curve for members that omit motion. Motion

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.process
entries.text: How the members run — sequential (each starts when the previous finishes) or simultaneous (all together). The one control unique to a group. sequential | simultaneous

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.relative
entries.text: The default offset-vs-absolute mode for members that omit relative. boolean

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.started
entries.text: Set true to run the whole group. boolean

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.paused
entries.text: Freeze/resume the group without resetting. boolean

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.start
entries.text: Runs the whole group (sequencing or paralleling its members per process) — the imperative equivalent of started = true. start(): void

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.stop
entries.text: Halts the group and all its members in place. Members keep their current values; nothing rewinds. stop(): void

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.start
entries.text: Fires once when the group begins — after its members are sequenced, not per member. onStart()

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.stop
entries.text: Fires once when the last member finishes, so it means the whole group is done — the place to chain the next thing. onStop()

entries.title: AnimatorGroup.repeat
entries.text: Fires at each loop of a repeating group (the outer group's repeat, not a member's). onRepeat()

entries.title: Spring
entries.text: The follow half of the animation family: drives its attribute toward a live, reactive to with spring physics — re-settling whenever to changes, and sleeping at rest (zero cost while idle). Use it wherever the target keeps moving: a cursor trail, a header that springs in on scroll, a value that chases wherever data puts it. Contrast Animator, which runs a fixed from→to and stops. It descends from Animator, so it inherits attribute and to; its own knobs are the spring constants. dot: View [ width = 10, height = 10, cornerRadius = 5, fill = turquoise, followX: Spring [ attribute = x, to = { app.pointerX - 5 }, stiffness = 120, damping = 14, mass = 0.6 ] ]

entries.title: Spring.stiffness
entries.text: Spring stiffness — higher pulls to the target faster (and can overshoot). The "how eager" knob. number

entries.title: Spring.damping
entries.text: Damping — higher settles with less bounce. Low damping + high stiffness gives a springy overshoot; high damping gives a smooth glide with none. number

entries.title: Spring.mass
entries.text: The moving mass — heavier trails more slowly, for a looser, longer follow (a lagging cursor dot). number

entries.title: Spring.epsilon
entries.text: The rest threshold: how close to to counts as at rest, at which point the spring sleeps (and stops costing anything). Larger = sleeps sooner, at the price of stopping a hair short. number

entries.title: Heartbeat
entries.text: The frame heartbeat as a member: calls your onFrame(dt) once per animation frame, with dt the real elapsed time in seconds. Spring and Animator are the declarative half of motion — say where a thing belongs and the runtime finds the path; Heartbeat is the raw tick an app that integrates something itself needs: custom gesture physics, a simulation, a game loop. Reach for it only when you are doing the integration; for "move this there, smoothly," a Spring is less code and better behaved. Before a Heartbeat, ask which of the other two you are about to re-implement. A value that should arrive somewhere is a Spring (target → value). A value that should advance — a replay cursor sweeping a day in ninety seconds, a progress that runs 0→1 — is an Animator (time → value): it is scrubbable, pausable, and interruptible for free, and everything that derives from it (seventy glyph opacities, a rule) follows with no per-frame code. A Heartbeat is right only when the next value depends on the last in a way no curve states — a body under forces, a particle system, a gesture you integrate yourself. In practice a Heartbeat in a program is worth a second look: it is usually one of the other two in disguise, and the per-frame handler it carries is where the program's only imperative state tends to collect. It rides the one shared clock every animator uses, so it costs nothing until it runs and never starts a second frame loop, and its lifetime is the node's — a discarded subtree cannot leave a loop running behind it. dt is clamped (a backgrounded tab resumes with a plausible step, not one enormous jump that would launch any integrator into the weeds). App [ width = 240, height = 120, fill = midnightblue, textColor = whitesmoke, x0: number = 20, v: number = 60, physics: Heartbeat [ onFrame(dt: number) { app.x0 = (app.x0 + app.v dt) % 200 } ], dot: View [ x = { app.x0 }, y = 40, width = 40, height = 40, cornerRadius = 20, fill = turquoise ] ]

entries.title: Heartbeat.running
entries.text: Is the heartbeat live? A plain reactive slot, so the usual idiom is a constraint — running = { app.simulating } — which starts and stops the loop as the app's own state changes. The first frame after a start establishes the time baseline and reports no step. boolean

entries.title: Heartbeat.frame
entries.text: onFrame(dt) — one call per animation frame while running, with the seconds elapsed since the previous frame. onFrame(dt: number)

entries.title: Keys
entries.text: The keyboard, as a member. Keys names one concept that a program can either ask or listen to: Keys.isDown("KeyA") is a call you make from any { } body; a Keys [ … ] member is how the keyboard calls you. It is the RAW stream — it fires even while a text field has focus, so gate app-level shortcuts on app state where that matters. A focused view's own onKeyDown/onKeyUp handlers are the other half of the story, and usually the right one for keys that belong to a particular widget. Lifetime is the node's: subscribed at init, dropped when the node is discarded, nothing to clean up. Fan-out is by instance — a menu, a dialog, and a menubar each holding a Keys member all hear the keyboard at once. App [ width = 240, height = 100, fill = white, textColor = black, n: number = 0, keys: Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { if (e.key == "ArrowUp") { app.n = app.n + 1 } else if (e.key == "ArrowDown") { app.n = app.n - 1 } } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 30, fontSize = 30, text = { n = ${n} } ] ]

entries.title: Keys.isDown
entries.text: Whether a key is physically down right now, by code ("ShiftLeft", "MetaLeft") — for modifier state at the moment of a gesture, which is not carried on a pointer event. How a table decides whether a click extends a range or toggles one member. onClick() { (parent as Table).rowClick(this.rowIndex(), this.member(), Keys.isDown("MetaLeft") Keys.isDown("ControlLeft"), Keys.isDown("ShiftLeft")) } isDown(code: string): boolean

entries.title: Keys.held
entries.text: Every key currently down, as code strings. held(): string[]

entries.title: Keys.navClaim
entries.text: Claims the navigation keys — arrows, Space, Home/End, Page — away from the browser's scroll defaults while an overlay is roving, and releases them when passed false. An open menu owns the arrow keys ; without the claim the page scrolls underneath it. Claim on open, release on close, always in pairs — a claim that outlives its overlay leaves the page unscrollable. navClaim(owner: object, on: boolean): void

entries.title: Keys.keyDown
entries.text: onKeyDown(e) — a key went down. e is a normalized KeyEvent: e.key ("ArrowUp", "Escape", "a"), e.code, and modifier flags — never a numeric code. onKeyDown(e: KeyEvent)

entries.title: Keys.keyUp
entries.text: onKeyUp(e) — a key came up, same payload. onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent)

entries.title: Focus
entries.text: The focus service, as a member. Like Keys, Focus names one concept a program can ask (Focus.focus(this), Focus.byKeyboard() — calls from any { } body) or listen to (a Focus [ … ] member). Listening is what a focus indicator does: the library's FocusRing follows focus with exactly these two handlers, tracking where focus went and the live silhouette of whatever holds it. Most apps never need it — focus rings, tab order, and activation are provided — but replacing the indicator is a supported thing to do, and this is how. watch: Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { classroot.target = v }, onGeometry(g: FocusGeometry) { classroot.tx = g.x; classroot.ty = g.y } ]

entries.title: Focus.focus
entries.text: Moves keyboard focus to a view — the only way to move it; assigning a control's focused does not. The call every control makes on pointer-down, so that the keyboard picks up where the pointer left off. Focusing a view that is not focusable is a no-op. onPointerDown() { Focus.focus(this) } focus(v: unknown): void

entries.title: Focus.blur
entries.text: Clears focus entirely, so nothing holds it. blur(): void

entries.title: Focus.next
entries.text: Moves focus to the next view in traversal order — what Tab does, callable directly when a control wants to advance focus itself (a field that moves on Enter). next(): void

entries.title: Focus.prev
entries.text: Moves focus to the previous view in traversal order — Shift-Tab's action. prev(): void

entries.title: Focus.byKeyboard
entries.text: Whether the current focus arrived by keyboard rather than by pointer — the web's :focus-visible rule, as a reactive read. This is what lets a clicked control show no focus edge while a tabbed one does, and what a focus indicator keys off to decide whether to appear at all. byKeyboard(): boolean

entries.title: Focus.getFocus
entries.text: The view that currently holds focus, or null — for saving focus before opening a modal and restoring it after. Restore on a later turn, not immediately: an in-flight keystroke must finish against the old focus, or the key that closed a dialog is delivered to the opener, which reopens it. getFocus(): any

entries.title: Focus.focusChange
entries.text: onFocusChange(v) — focus moved to view v (or null when nothing is focused). onFocusChange(v: View)

entries.title: Focus.geometry
entries.text: onGeometry(g) — the focused control's live root-space silhouette: g.x, g.y, g.w, g.h, g.rad (its corner radius), g.view, and g.root (the app that owns it — an embedded app's ring ignores a target belonging to another). onGeometry(g: FocusGeometry)

entries.title: Tip
entries.text: The tooltip service, as a member: onTip(e) fires when a view carrying tip = "…" wants its tooltip shown, and with null when it should hide. The service owns the platform conventions — the show delay, instant retarget while showing, hide on press — so a listener only renders. The library's Tooltip is the one listener most programs ever need, and it arrives automatically in any app whose views carry tips. Declare your own Tip [ … ] member only when you are replacing that rendition. tips: Tip [ onTip(e: TipEvent) { if (e == null) { classroot.shown = false; return } classroot.label = e.text classroot.shown = true } ]

entries.title: Tip.tip
entries.text: onTip(e) — show the tip described by e (e.text, plus the target's root-space box e.x/e.y/e.w/e.h and its owning app e.root), or hide when e is null. onTip(e: TipEvent)

entries.title: Stream
entries.text: The abstract base of the live-connection sources — EventStream (SSE) and Socket (WebSocket) extend it. Not instantiable: write the concrete transport. The one thing to know: there is no connect() or disconnect() — the declaration decides. A stream is connected exactly while active is true and url is non-empty; empty the url (or flip active) and it closes, change the url and it closes and reopens, remove the node and the connection dies with it. Nothing to unsubscribe, ever. Messages are transient: nothing accumulates unless a handler writes it somewhere — the runtime keeps only last. An app that streams JSON parses in the handler (JSON.parse(e.data)) and writes wherever it wants; accumulation is one line of app code, deliberately not a built-in policy. chat: View [ answer: string = "", reply: EventStream [ url = { /api/chat?id=${classroot.chatId} }, active = { classroot.chatId != "" }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { classroot.answer = classroot.answer + e.data }, ], out: Text [ width = { parent.width }, text = { parent.answer } ] ]

entries.title: Stream.url
entries.text: Where to connect — a literal or a { } constraint. Unlike DataSource.url, a change acts immediately: the old connection closes and a new one opens at the new address (there is no fetch() moment to wait for). "" means detached — the idiom for "no conversation yet" is deriving emptiness: url = { app.chatId != "" ? "/api/chat/" + app.chatId : "" }. string

entries.title: Stream.active
entries.text: The gate. false closes the connection (and cancels any pending retry); flipping back true reopens it. Bind it to app state — active = { app.live } — rather than toggling imperatively. boolean

entries.title: Stream.retry
entries.text: Reconnect policy, visible in the declaration: seconds to wait before re-dialing after the connection is lost and the platform won't bring it back on its own — a Socket's unexpected close, an EventStream's terminal failure. 0 (the default) means no retry: the stream lands in status = "failed" and the app decides. A declared retry keeps trying while active is true, at a fixed interval — no invisible backoff, no give-up count. A structural failure (the factory itself refuses — headless extraction, a missing host service) never loops, whatever retry says. number

entries.title: Stream.status
entries.text: The connection lifecycle as one fact, like DataSource.status: "closed", "connecting", "open", "retrying", or "failed" (down, and will not reconnect). Read-only — computed for you; assigning it is a compile error. "retrying" covers both the platform's own recovery (SSE) and a declared retry waiting to re-dial. closed | connecting | open | retrying | failed

entries.title: Stream.error
entries.text: The last failure reason, "" when none; cleared when a connection opens. Read-only — the state side of onError (the event side). A status line is text = { feed.error != "" ? feed.error : feed.status }. string

entries.title: Stream.last
entries.text: The most recent message's data, reactive. Read-only. The zero-handler tier: a ticker that only shows the latest value needs no handler at all — text = { feed.last }. string

entries.title: Stream.open
entries.text: The boolean view of status == "open", as DataSource.loaded is of its status — one fact, two spellings, never in disagreement. Read-only. The connection dot is visible = { feed.open }. boolean

entries.title: Stream.message
entries.text: onMessage(e: StreamMessage) — every message. e.data is always a string: parse it yourself if it is JSON, concatenate it if it is streamed text; the runtime never guesses. e.type is the SSE named event ("message" for unnamed messages and every socket frame); e.id is the SSE last-event-id ("" on sockets). onMessage(e: StreamMessage)

entries.title: Stream.open
entries.text: The connection is live — fires each time one opens, including reopens after a retry. Prefer deriving from open/status for anything a constraint can express; the handler is for work state cannot do (send a subscription frame, log). onOpen()

entries.title: Stream.close
entries.text: A connection that had opened went away — the app closed it (active, a url change, node removal at discard is silent), the server ended it, or it failed. Fires once per connection, before any retry dials the next one. onClose()

entries.title: Stream.error
entries.text: Something failed: a terminal connection loss, a refused transport, a send on a socket that is not open. The reason is in error when the handler runs. The platform's own in-flight retries (SSE) are not errors and stay quiet. onError()

entries.title: EventStream
entries.text: Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream) as a source — the streaming-AI shape: the server pushes, the app receives, an onMessage that concatenates is the whole consumer. See Stream for the shared surface (url/active/retry, the read-only status/open/error/last). Receive-only — there is no send; a request that needs a body is an ordinary DataSource POST, and the stream carries the reply. The platform's EventSource machinery is kept verbatim: it retries on its own (honoring the server's retry: hint) and resumes with Last-Event-ID, during which status reads "retrying" and no error is reported; retry/onError concern only terminal failure — the platform giving up. A declared stream holds a live connection for as long as it is active and its node lives — every open tab is one held server connection (browsers cap ~6 per host over HTTP/1.1, so a dev server's tabs can exhaust the pool). The lifecycle is the declaration: active = { app.chatId != "" } releases the connection the moment the condition goes false, and a discarded node closes its own — there is nothing to unsubscribe. answer: string = "", reply: EventStream [ url = { /api/chat?id=${app.chatId} }, active = { app.chatId != "" }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.answer = app.answer + e.data }, ]

entries.title: EventStream.listenTo
entries.text: The named SSE event types to deliver — listenTo = ["contentblockdelta", "message_stop"]. Required for any stream that labels messages with event: lines (Anthropic-style AI streams do): the platform's EventSource physically cannot deliver a named event it was not asked to listen for, so an undeclared name is silently invisible — if onMessage sees nothing but the connection is open, this is the first thing to check. The name carries the contract: you hear what you listen to. Unnamed (default) messages always arrive; e.type says which kind each one is. array

entries.title: Socket
entries.text: WebSocket as a source: the Stream surface plus send(text) — send is a call you make, onMessage is it calling you. See Stream for url/active/retry and the read-only status/open/error/last. Unlike SSE the platform has no native reconnect, so a Socket that should survive a dropped connection must say so: retry = 2 re-dials two seconds after any close the app didn't ask for, for as long as active holds — the whole policy is that one number. Text frames only; a binary frame is dropped (a later attribute if a real project needs one, not a speculative shape now). live: Socket [ url = "wss://api.example.com/feed", retry = 2, onOpen() { this.send('{"subscribe":"prices"}') }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.tick(JSON.parse(e.data)) }, ]

entries.title: Socket.send
entries.text: Sends one text frame. Legal only while open — on a socket that is not open it sends nothing and reports through the error channel (error + onError), never a silent queue: if the app needs buffering-until-connected, that policy belongs in app state, visibly. Sending the opening frame belongs in onOpen (which also covers every reconnect); gate user-triggered sends on .open. send(text: string): void

entries.title: State
entries.text: A named bundle of overrides that snaps on and off together. Its body is not ordinary children: a name = value entry is an override of the enclosing view's own attribute (checked against that view's schema, not the State's), applied while the state is on; an id: Type [ … ] entry is a conditional subtree that exists only while applied. Because attribute reads compose as a precedence stack, the base values return exactly when the state turns off — there is no manual undo to write, and no drift. card: View [ height = 72, fill = white, open: State [ applied = { expanded }, height = 184, fill = lightsteelblue, Text [ text = "shown only while open" ] ] ]

entries.title: State.applied
entries.text: Whether the state is on. Bind it to a condition (applied = { expanded }) and the whole bundle snaps in and out as that flips — the base values restore themselves when it turns off. The declarative alternative to the apply() / remove() / toggle() verbs. boolean

entries.title: State.apply
entries.text: Turns the bundle on imperatively — the verb form of applied = true. Prefer binding applied to a condition; reach for apply() only when the toggle is truly event-driven and has no natural boolean to bind. apply(): void

entries.title: State.remove
entries.text: Turns the bundle off, restoring the base values via the precedence stack (no manual undo). The partner of apply(). remove(): void

entries.title: State.toggle
entries.text: Flips the bundle on/off from its current state — a one-call switch for a handler (onClick() { panel.toggle() }) when you don't want to thread a boolean. toggle(): void

entries.title: State.apply
entries.text: Fires when the bundle turns on — after the overrides compose onto the stack, so reads in the handler already see the state's values. Use for a side effect that must ride with the state (focus a revealed field), not to mutate what the state already declares. onApply()

entries.title: State.remove
entries.text: Fires when the bundle turns off, the partner of onApply — after the base values have restored. For tearing down whatever onApply set up. onRemove()

entries.title: Node
entries.text: The plain object-graph atom — a non-visual node you subclass for logic that isn't a view: a controller, a coordinator, a service. A bare class X [ … ] defaults its base to Node, so a class with attributes and methods but no box is a Node subclass. It lives in the tree as a named member, shares the reactive core and the classroot/app reach, and fires init — but it paints nothing. Reach for it instead of a View when a wrapper class would be visual in name only. class Cart [ count: number = 0, add() { count = count + 1 }, clear() { count = 0 } ] A view then holds one as a named member (cart: Cart [ ]) and reads/drives it reactively — state and behaviour with no pixels of its own.

entries.title: Node.init
entries.text: Fires once when the node has finished constructing and its subtree exists — the place for setup that needs the built tree. Every node gets it, faceless subclasses included (the init walk covers non-View children since 2026-08-20 — before that, only views were visited and a Node's onInit silently never fired). Answered by onInit(). onInit()

entries.title: Bar
entries.text: A labeled horizontal value bar: an optional caption, then a rounded track filled to value. A placeholder component (composition.md §1a) — coherent and restyleable, but not the final widget. For a themed, theme-tracking meter reach for ProgressBar instead; Bar exists for demos and dashboards that want a caption and their own colour. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], Bar [ width = 260, label = "Storage", value = 72 ], Bar [ width = 260, label = "Memory", value = 38, tint = #37E0C8 ] ]

entries.title: Bar.label
entries.text: The caption to the left of the track. "" drops the caption column entirely and the track takes the full width. string

entries.title: Bar.value
entries.text: How full the track reads, 0–100 always — a percentage, not your own units. This is the difference from ProgressBar, which takes min/max and lets you pass raw counts. number

entries.title: Bar.tint
entries.text: The fill colour. The one restyling knob — Bar predates the theme tokens and carries literal defaults, so it does not follow a theme the way library controls do. Color

entries.title: Bar.lead
entries.text: The caption column's width, derived from whether there is a label at all. Set it to align several bars whose captions differ in length. number

entries.title: Control
entries.text: The interaction-state base every stateful control extends (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 3). It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and nothing semantic: checked, value, and their kin live on the concrete control. The pointer half is the language's now: hovered and pressed are View's read-only interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe). What Control adds is the CONTROL policy on top of them, as derivations every concrete control reads: hot / down — the styling pair: the intrinsics gated by disabled, with the keyboard-activation flash folded into down. Style against these, not the raw intrinsics, and a disabled control never lights up. disabled — inert: not focusable, no activation; concrete controls gate on it. keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same press() path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look. It also owns the two things every labelled control was improvising: iconLeft / iconRight — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays them out; Control only declares that they exist, so Button and Segment answer to one vocabulary. menu — the ROLE of dropping a menu. Not decoration: fifteen sites across the corpus call someMenu.openFor(control), and the disclosure mark for that one role was drawn five different ways or omitted (a glyph inside the label string in five places, a private chevron in two, a separate Text in one, nothing in MenuBar and DataGrid). Nobody chose those differences. Setting menu gets the mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and Down-to-open together, which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong one piece at a time. Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated, and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships: class Stepper extends Control [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, n: number = 0, fill = { down ? theme.controlPressed : hot ? theme.controlHover : theme.control }, press() { n = n + 1 }, onClick() { if (!disabled) press() }, t: Text [ x = center, y = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ] ] App [ Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]

entries.title: Control.disabled
entries.text: Inert: not focusable, no activation, and the gate folded into hot/down so a disabled control never lights up. Constrain it rather than assigning it (disabled = { app.muted }) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also dim themselves against theme.disabledOpacity. boolean

entries.title: Control.focused
entries.text: True while this control holds keyboard focus. For the ring, you want nothing: the app-level FocusRing indicates focus for you. Read this only for a control's own focus styling. boolean

entries.title: Control.hot
entries.text: Hover under control policy — hovered gated by disabled. Style against this, not the raw hovered intrinsic , or a disabled control lights up under the pointer. Always false on touch, since hovered is. boolean

entries.title: Control.down
entries.text: The pressed look — the pressed intrinsic gated by disabled, with keyboard activation folded in , so Space/Enter flashes the same appearance a pointer press gives. The other half of the styling pair with hot. boolean

entries.title: Control.focusVisible
entries.text: Focused and the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's :focus-visible channel. Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a Pane header's focus edge reads. boolean

entries.title: Control.iconLeft
entries.text: A decorative icon for the leading slot, named by class (iconLeft = "TrashIcon"), not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored and data-bound are the same mechanism (iconLeft = { "" + :icon } in a replicated toolbar). Control only declares the slot; the concrete control lays it out. A computed name needs use [ Name ] to survive the build, since no static reference reaches it. string

entries.title: Control.iconRight
entries.text: The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as iconLeft. Setting it wins over the chevron a menu would imply — see rightIcon. string

entries.title: Control.menu
entries.text: The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (menu = { app.optionsMenu }). Setting it is a role, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. Declare one menu and point many controls at it rather than one per opener; the menu reads opener to vary its items. View

entries.title: Control.menuOpen
entries.text: True while menu is showing and this control is what opened it. Derived, never written — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way (Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open look forever. boolean

entries.title: Control.rightIcon
entries.text: What actually renders on the right: iconRight when set, else the disclosure chevron implied by menu, else nothing. One place decides, so every menu-dropping control in the corpus wears the same mark. string

entries.title: Control.flash
entries.text: The keyboard-activation pulse — the control's own state, since the pressed intrinsic is the pointer's truth and is read-only. Folded into down, so styling needs to read only the pair. boolean

entries.title: Control.flashMs
entries.text: How long flashPress() holds the pressed look. number

entries.title: Control.openMenu
entries.text: Opens menu anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled. The seam a concrete control calls from its own press(). openMenu()

entries.title: Control.press
entries.text: The activation seam — override this, not the handlers. Pointer and keyboard both land here, so one override serves a click, Space, and Enter. The base opens menu when there is one. A value control delivers through input from here and never writes its own value slot directly , which is what lets a bound control avoid fighting its constraint. press()

entries.title: Control.focusShape
entries.text: The focus silhouette the ring hugs, { x, y, w, h, rad } in this control's own coordinates. null (the default) rings the whole bounds at its cornerRadius. Override to ring the part that means something — a Radio rings its dot, a Slider its thumb. focusShape()

entries.title: Control.flashPress
entries.text: Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention for buttons and menu items. Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback (Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it. flashPress()

entries.title: Control.focus
entries.text: Records focus and captures the keyboard modality into focusVisible. An override must keep both or the focus channel goes dark. onFocus()

entries.title: Control.blur
entries.text: Clears focused and focusVisible. onBlur()

entries.title: Control.pointerDown
entries.text: Claims focus, clears the :focus-visible channel, and opens menu if there is one — menus open on press, not release, as the platform does. An override must keep the Focus.focus(this) call , or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere. onPointerDown()

entries.title: Control.keyDown
entries.text: Space and Enter run press(); ArrowDown opens menu. Ignores auto-repeat. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: Checkbox
entries.text: A boolean control (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 1). Its value is the checked attribute; input owns the value's destination — by default the destination is the checkbox itself, so it works standalone with zero wiring: mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ] … visible = { mute.checked } Hand the value to its real owner by overriding input and constraining down: Checkbox [ label = "Mute", checked = { app.muted }, input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v } ] press() never writes checked directly — it only delivers — so a bound checkbox never fights its constraint. row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ], Text [ text = { mute.checked ? "muted" : "audible" } ] ]

entries.title: Checkbox.checked
entries.text: Whether the box is ticked. Standalone it owns this and you read it back by name; bound (checked = { app.muted }) it needs an input override to go with it — a one-way binding with no input leaves the checkbox's own edit assigning to a constrained slot, which is refused at runtime. boolean

entries.title: Checkbox.label
entries.text: The text beside the box. "" renders the box alone — the form for a checkbox inside a table cell, where the column heading is the label. string

entries.title: Checkbox.size
entries.text: The box's edge length. Defaults to the theme's figure, so a toolbar checkbox can shrink to match its neighbours without a subclass. number

entries.title: Checkbox.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the box alone, not the box-plus-label — the Radio rule, so a long label does not drag a wide ring across the row. focusShape()

entries.title: Checkbox.input
entries.text: Where the value goes. The default writes checked; override it and the checkbox becomes a delivery channel for state you own (input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v }). This is the one member to override when the value lives elsewhere. input(v)

entries.title: Checkbox.press
entries.text: Toggles by delivering the flipped value through input — never by writing checked, which is what keeps a bound checkbox from fighting its constraint. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Checkbox.click
entries.text: Runs press() when enabled. Override input instead if what you want is the value. onClick()

entries.title: Button
entries.text: A labeled action control. The action is its onClick — write it at the use site exactly as on any View; Button adds the interaction states, the themed look, and keyboard activation (Space/Enter drives the same onClick). primary = true fills with the accent; the default is the quiet control look. Button [ label = "Save" ] Button [ label = "Delete", iconLeft = "TrashIcon" ] Button [ label = "Options", menu = { app.optionsMenu } ] // chevron implied Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ] // icon only Three slots in a row — iconLeft, the label, iconRight — laid out by SimpleLayout and sized from contentWidth, so an absent label or icon costs nothing and needs no special case: an invisible child is skipped and its space reclaimed. A menu supplies the right icon on its own (control.declare). The fill walks the four-rung ladder — control at rest, controlHover, controlPressed, and controlSelected while its menu is open. Before the ladder existed this read down hot ? controlActive : control, which meant hovering a button looked exactly like pressing it .

entries.title: Button.label
entries.text: The button's text. "" (the default) leaves it iconless-and-wordless, which is only useful with an icon — a button with neither has nothing to press. string

entries.title: Button.primary
entries.text: Marks this as the affirmative action: it fills with the accent and takes theme.accentText for its ink. One per group of choices — a dialog's Save, not its Cancel. Purely a style decision; it changes nothing about behaviour. boolean

entries.title: Button.gap
entries.text: Space between the icon and the label, when both are present. number

entries.title: Button.padH
entries.text: Horizontal padding inside the button, each side. The button sizes to its content plus twice this, so widening it is how you make a short label less cramped. number

entries.title: Button.inkColor
entries.text: The one ink decision, so a button's icon and its label always agree: the accent text colour when primary, the ordinary text colour otherwise. textColor follows it. Override this rather than textColor alone, or the icon and the words drift apart. Color

entries.title: Button.press
entries.text: The activation path, called by a click and by Space/Enter. It flashes the press tint, opens an attached menu if there is one, then calls onClick. Override onClick for ordinary use; override this only to change what activation means. press()

entries.title: Button.click
entries.text: Your handler. Fires after the press is delivered, so the affordance has already run — put the work here, not in press(). onClick()

entries.title: Switch
entries.text: A boolean control with a sliding thumb — same value contract as Checkbox (checked, input owns the destination), different body language: the thumb SPRINGS between its two rest points, so toggling moves rather than jumps.

entries.title: Switch.checked
entries.text: Whether the switch is on. Bind it (checked = { app.muted }) and override input to own the destination, or leave it and read it back — a Switch works standalone with no wiring. boolean

entries.title: Switch.input
entries.text: Where the value goes. The default writes checked; override it and the switch becomes a delivery mechanism for state you own. press() never writes checked directly, so a bound switch never fights its constraint. input(v)

entries.title: Switch.press
entries.text: Toggles, by delivering the flipped value through input. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Switch.click
entries.text: Fires on click when the switch is enabled. press() is the activation path; prefer overriding input if what you want is the value. onClick()

entries.title: Slider
entries.text: A bounded number by drag (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 1). Same value contract as every control — value is the attribute, input owns the destination (default: itself) — and the delivery is CONTINUOUS during a drag (ruled: the owner decides what to do with the stream; the data layer owns coalescing). Pressing the track jumps to that position (local coordinates); the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta (app.pointerX — the captured-move pattern the calendar's drag uses). Arrow keys nudge by step. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], vol: Slider [ value = 40 ], Text [ text = { volume ${Math.round(vol.value)} } ] ]

entries.title: Slider.value
entries.text: Where the handle sits, in your own units. Standalone the slider owns it; bound (value = { app.volume }) it needs an input override with it, or the drag's own delivery is refused against the constraint. number

entries.title: Slider.min
entries.text: The value at the left end. number

entries.title: Slider.max
entries.text: The value at the right end. number

entries.title: Slider.step
entries.text: The quantum every delivered value snaps to, and the distance one arrow key moves. step = 0.01 for a fine continuous control; it is never zero — the quantizer divides by it. number

entries.title: Slider.frac
entries.text: The handle's position as 0…1, derived from the value and the range. What the track, fill, and thumb all position from; read it to hang your own decoration off the handle. number

entries.title: Slider.dragging
entries.text: True from pointer-down until the captured release. The pressed intrinsic deliberately will not do here — it is hit-chain-based, so it goes false the moment the pointer leaves the thumb, while a drag must survive exactly that. boolean

entries.title: Slider.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the circular grabber — the part the arrow keys move — rather than the whole track. focusShape()

entries.title: Slider.input
entries.text: Where the value goes, and it fires continuously through a drag, not once at release: the owner decides what to do with the stream, and the data layer owns any coalescing. Override it to redirect the value (input(v: number) { app.volume = v }); the default writes value. input(v)

entries.title: Slider.quant
entries.text: Snaps a raw value to step and clamps it into min…max. Every delivery routes through it, so an override changes what the slider can produce — logarithmic scales, detents, a magnetic centre. quant(v)

entries.title: Slider.barStyle
entries.text: True when the theme asks for the Material-3 rendition: a vertical bar handle with the track shortened either side of it rather than drawn through. One theme token (theme.sliderHandle) selects a rendition — data, not a fork. barStyle()

entries.title: Slider.dotStyle
entries.text: True for the Fluent rendition: a round grabber with an accent dot inside that grows under hover and press. The other value of the same token. dotStyle()

entries.title: Slider.pointerDown
entries.text: Jumps the value to the pressed position, claims focus, and latches the drag. onPointerDown(e)

entries.title: Slider.pointerUp
entries.text: Ends the drag. onPointerUp()

entries.title: Slider.pointerMove
entries.text: Tracks the drag by root-space pointer delta, so the handle keeps up with a pointer that has left the control. onPointerMove()

entries.title: Slider.keyDown
entries.text: Left and Right nudge by one step, delivered through input like any other change. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: RadioGroup
entries.text: One-of-N (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 1 — ruled: the GROUP owns the bindable value; radios deliver to it, the ViewTab → app.mode shape). Radios are written as the group's DIRECT children — the group's layout arranges them, and each radio reaches its group as parent: RadioGroup [ value = "m", input(v: string) { app.size = v }, Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ], ] size: RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = "m", Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ] ]

entries.title: RadioGroup.value
entries.text: The group's value — the chosen choice, and the only value slot in the pair. A Radio has none of its own; it derives on from this. Standalone the group owns it; bound, override input beside it as with any control. string

entries.title: RadioGroup.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes. The default writes value; override it to own the destination (input(v: string) { app.size = v }) and the radios keep working untouched, because they deliver rather than store. input(v)

entries.title: RadioGroup.pick
entries.text: Selects a choice by name — the seam a Radio calls on its group. Call it to move the selection from code without bypassing input. pick(v)

entries.title: Radio
entries.text: One-of-N (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 1 — ruled: the GROUP owns the bindable value; radios deliver to it, the ViewTab → app.mode shape). Radios are written as the group's DIRECT children — the group's layout arranges them, and each radio reaches its group as parent: RadioGroup [ value = "m", input(v: string) { app.size = v }, Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ], ] size: RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = "m", Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ] ]

entries.title: Radio.choice
entries.text: This radio's identity within its group, compared against the group's value by string. Required and unique per group — two radios sharing a choice light together. string

entries.title: Radio.label
entries.text: The text beside the dot. "" renders the dot alone. string

entries.title: Radio.on
entries.text: Whether this radio is the group's current choice. Derived from the group, never stored — which is why turning one on cannot leave another stale. boolean

entries.title: Radio.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the round dot rather than the dot-plus-label row — the ruled rendition. focusShape()

entries.title: Radio.press
entries.text: Delivers this radio's choice to the group. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Radio.click
entries.text: Runs press() when enabled. onClick()

entries.title: Field
entries.text: A labeled form row: the label column, then whatever control the use site nests (its DIRECT child, arranged by the row's layout): Field [ label = "Name", TextInput [ width = 220, height = 30 ] ] labelWidth is the shared-column knob (Contract 4, ruled: a form wanting aligned labels sets ONE plain value and each row constrains to it — never aggregation, which the constraint system forbids by design). A note/error line under the control is DEFERRED: routing use-site children into named regions is the §13 slots/placement open — this component is Tier 1's concrete evidence for that item's priority. form: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], Field [ label = "Name", TextInput [ width = 200, height = 28 ] ], Field [ label = "Notify", Switch [ ] ] ]

entries.title: Field.label
entries.text: The caption in the left column. It is a Text, not a control's own label — a Field labels whatever you nest, so the nested control's own label should usually be empty or you will render the words twice. string

entries.title: Field.labelWidth
entries.text: The label column's width, and the knob that aligns a form. Every row in a form sets the same plain number — one value, repeated or read from a shared attribute (labelWidth = { app.formLabels }). It is deliberately not measured from the widest label: aggregating over sibling rows is exactly what the constraint system refuses, so the shared column is a value you state rather than one the form discovers. number

entries.title: ProgressBar
entries.text: Display-only bounded number — the read-only sibling of Slider (same value/ min/max vocabulary, no interaction, no input). Restyle by theme; impose a width per the interior contract.

entries.title: ProgressBar.value
entries.text: Where the bar sits, in the units you choose. Clamped into min…max for display, so a value outside the range renders full or empty rather than overflowing. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.min
entries.text: The value that reads as empty. Defaults to 0. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.max
entries.text: The value that reads as full. Defaults to 100 — set it to your own total and pass raw counts as value rather than converting to a percentage yourself. number

entries.title: FocusRing
entries.text: The traveling focus indicator — the OpenLaszlo 3.4 focusoverlay line, on the reactive core, at its third form: a SHAPE-HUGGING rounded outline whose terminus reshapes to the focused control's own silhouette (library-charter §6 — the ring springs position, size, AND cornerRadius; a Radio's row ring, a pill Switch's ring, and a text field's ring differ because the targets do). The layered model (charter, ratified): The fact — the ring listens to Focus (a Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { … } ] member) and tracks the target's root-space geometry on EVERY change, pointer or keyboard. A pointer focus PARKS the ring there silently (snap, no show) — so the next Tab's flight departs from the control the user just clicked, never from a stale perch. Roles, theme-elected — theme.focusRing: "both" (or true, the default) · "travel" (flight + the OL idle fade) · "rest" (no flight — the ring appears in place and stays) · false (no ring; the theme's components carry the at-rest indication — the invariant lives with the THEME+components pair). While keyboard modality holds and the role includes rest, the ring RESTS — no idle fade; a pointer press clears modality and the ring hides (web :focus-visible semantics). The flight is the flourish — theme.focusAnimate = false (the sampler's "Animate focus transitions" toggle) snaps every move; the underdamped travel is default-on. It arrives automatically with any Control-descended component (the OL canvas.focusclass default); declare your own FocusRing [ ] (or subclass) to replace it. Pure chrome: never focusable, never a pointer target. (v1 limits, recorded: root-space bounds are summed through the parent chain — a scrolled container is not compensated; the silhouette is the target's cornerRadius — a focusShape() override protocol arrives with the emulation passes.) You do not instantiate this, and you do not position it. Tab between the controls below and watch it fly; the members exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition, and for the theme tokens that elect its behaviour. row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 12 ], Button [ label = "One" ], Button [ label = "Two" ], Checkbox [ label = "Three" ] ]

entries.title: FocusRing.overlayUp
entries.text: True while an overlay owns the keyboard (an open Menu). The ring stands down — the menu's own rover is the focus story, and a page ring poking around a panel reads as chrome fighting chrome. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.shown
entries.text: Whether the ring is visible. A pointer focus parks it silently — geometry current, ring hidden — so the next Tab departs from the control the user just clicked rather than from a stale perch. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.placed
entries.text: Whether the ring has ever had a target to park on. The first appearance never flies, because a flight from nowhere is a streak across the app. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.idle
entries.text: True once a travel-role ring has sat still long enough to fade out — the OpenLaszlo idle behaviour. A resting ring never sets it. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.ringRole
entries.text: The theme's election, from theme.focusRing: "both" (the default), "travel" (flight plus the OpenLaszlo idle fade), "rest" (appears in place and stays, no flight), or "off". "off" is legitimate only when the theme's own controls carry an at-rest focus indication — the invariant belongs to the theme-and-components pair, not to the ring alone. ringRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.restRole
entries.text: Whether the elected role includes resting — a resting ring does not idle-fade. restRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.travelRole
entries.text: Whether the elected role includes the flight. travelRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.snapTo
entries.text: Lands the ring on its target immediately, skipping the flight. What a pointer focus, a first appearance, and theme.focusAnimate = false all use — and what a target moving under a resting ring uses , so a dragged slider thumb carries the ring rigidly instead of springing after it. snapTo()

entries.title: FocusRing.draw
entries.text: Renders the outline: four corner arcs with arms whose length is a pure function of distance from the target, so the physics does the choreography. Override to replace the rendition entirely. theme.focusSights = true restores the open-bracket "target sights" reading; theme.focusRingInnerWidth adds the Fluent two-tone band. draw(d)

entries.title: Accordion
entries.text: OpenLaszlo's basetabslider, reborn — stacked pane headers, one pane open at a time, panes SLIDING open and closed by a spring on height. The load-bearing mechanic (docs/system-design/tabslider-gaps.md, verified frame-by-frame against the original): a pane's content is PRESENT through the whole open and close, revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its height animates — never an instant pop, never a blank gap. Value contract (components-baseline.md): the open pane is ONE attribute on the group — value, the open pane's name — exactly RadioGroup's shape. Panes are the group's direct children; each names itself (name, defaulting to its label) and derives open from the group. Content is authored as the Pane's ordinary children — the Pane stacks its header then the content, and clips. Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, Pane [ label = "Account", initial = true, Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, wrap = true, text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ] ], Pane [ label = "Privacy", Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, text = "One pane open at a time." ] ] ]

entries.title: Accordion.value
entries.text: The open pane's name — the group's whole value, exactly RadioGroup's shape. Assign it to open a pane from code; "" closes all of them. A Pane never stores whether it is open, it derives it from here, which is why the one-open-at-a-time invariant cannot break. string

entries.title: Pane
entries.text: OpenLaszlo's basetabslider, reborn — stacked pane headers, one pane open at a time, panes SLIDING open and closed by a spring on height. The load-bearing mechanic (docs/system-design/tabslider-gaps.md, verified frame-by-frame against the original): a pane's content is PRESENT through the whole open and close, revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its height animates — never an instant pop, never a blank gap. Value contract (components-baseline.md): the open pane is ONE attribute on the group — value, the open pane's name — exactly RadioGroup's shape. Panes are the group's direct children; each names itself (name, defaulting to its label) and derives open from the group. Content is authored as the Pane's ordinary children — the Pane stacks its header then the content, and clips. Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, Pane [ label = "Account", initial = true, Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, wrap = true, text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ] ], Pane [ label = "Privacy", Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, text = "One pane open at a time." ] ] ]

entries.title: Pane.label
entries.text: The pane header's text, and — unless you set name — its identity in the group. string

entries.title: Pane.name
entries.text: This pane's identity, defaulting to its label. Set it when two panes share a label, or when the label is user-facing copy you expect to change , so the group's value does not move under you when the wording does. string

entries.title: Pane.initial
entries.text: Seeds the group: the first pane declaring initial = true opens if nothing else has claimed value yet. A one-shot at init, not a binding — to drive which pane is open from state, constrain the group's value instead . boolean

entries.title: Pane.open
entries.text: Whether this pane is the group's current one. Derived; read it to style your content. boolean

entries.title: Pane.twist
entries.text: The header chevron's angle, in radians, sprung between 0 and −π/2. It turns in step with the height animation rather than snapping , which is the whole reason it is a number and not a swap between two marks — a number can be sprung. number

entries.title: Pane.tabOrder
entries.text: Contributes the pane's contents to keyboard traversal only while it is open. A closed pane is clip-occluded rather than hidden — its content must stay visible for the slide to carry it — so this is what stops Tab from descending into a pane the user cannot see . The header itself remains a stop either way. tabOrder()

entries.title: Pane.press
entries.text: Opens this pane by writing its name to the group. Called by a click and by Space/Enter on the header. press()

entries.title: Pane.init
entries.text: Applies initial. Fires once per pane. onInit()

entries.title: Pane.click
entries.text: Runs press() when enabled. onClick()

entries.title: Tooltip
entries.text: The layer system's floor (planes.md §2, tier 1): any view sets tip = "…" and this singleton renders it — hover delay, placement, flip, and theming are nobody's problem at the use site. It arrives automatically when any view in the program carries a tip (the FocusRing auto-arrival mechanism); declare your own Tooltip [ ] (or subclass) to replace the rendition. It listens to the Tip service (a Tip [ onTip(e: TipEvent) { … } ] member), which owns the platform conventions (the show delay — tooltipDelay, ~1s in the Cupertino and Redmond conventions, ~500ms Material — instant retarget while showing, hide on press). PLACEMENT is theme data too (tooltipPlacement): "below" (the default — under the target, centered, flipping above at the edge), "above" (Fluent/WinUI's default, flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag — offset below-right of where the cursor rests). Always clamped inside the app. Pure chrome — never focusable, never a pointer target, always above content (the auto-splice puts it last in the App, and source order stacks). Theming (the four cities carry the tokens): tooltipBg / tooltipText / tooltipLine (null = no border) / tooltipSize (11 in Cupertino, 12 elsewhere). Cupertino and Redmond wear bordered surface chips; San Francisco and Mountain View the inverse chip. You do not instantiate this. Set tip on any view and the singleton appears; the members below exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition. View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 130, height = 38, cornerRadius = 8, fill = steelblue, tip = "Saves your changes", Text [ x = center, y = center, textColor = white, text = "Save" ] ]

entries.title: Tooltip.tipText
entries.text: The text currently displayed, pushed in by the Tip service from the hovered view's tip. A subclass reads this; nothing writes it from app code. string

entries.title: Tooltip.shown
entries.text: Whether a tip is currently up. Driven by the service's delay, retarget and hide rules — not by you. boolean

entries.title: Tooltip.placement
entries.text: Where the chip sits, elected by theme.tooltipPlacement: "below" (the default, centred under the target, flipping above at the edge), "above" (the Fluent default, flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag, offset below-right of the resting cursor). Always clamped inside the app. string

entries.title: Menu
entries.text: The record-driven menu (planes.md §4–§6): items are DATA — the component arranges; the author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS menus: { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? } key renders right-aligned (display only — registration is the Keys service's, later). icon: "ClassName" names an icon class for the leading column, and the label shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary Segmented's choices use. This was THREE mechanisms before the icon set landed: a text glyph ("◐"), a hardcoded "lightbulb" that special-cased its way to a drawn bulb because no glyph matched, and iconKind naming a class. The middle one was the tell — somebody needed a mark the fonts could not give, and the escape hatch already existed. One field now; a COMPUTED name needs its class kept with use [ Name ], since no static reference reaches it. enabled: false dims the row (theme.disabledOpacity) and refuses pick. { divider: true } is a separator line. submenu: [ …records… ] marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow; the cascade itself lands with the roving-keyboard stage). kind: "ClassName" renders the row's CONTENT with a named author class (app.createView — keep data-only classes with use [ Name ]), passed props as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight, pick, keyboard are the menu's, always. Declared ONCE, opened by many (the worked example): rows carry onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }; the menu's items constraint derives from opener — per-row variation with zero per-row instances, live while open. openAt point-positions (the context-menu rule); openFor drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both RAISE the menu (promotion — order is a slot) and clamp inside the app. Dismissal: the BACKDROP (a full-app child under the panel) — a press outside closes AND is swallowed, the Mac rule (planes.md §12.1, resolved for v1); Escape closes; pick closes after delivery. App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "", edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }), ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: Menu.items
entries.text: The rows, as records — never children. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? }; a plain array is fine (no Dataset required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it can be a constraint — derive it from opener and one menu serves every row of a table , live while it is open. array

entries.title: Menu.opener
entries.text: The view this menu was opened for, set by openAt/openFor and cleared on close. The key to declaring one menu and opening it from many places: read it in the items constraint to vary the rows per opener, with no per-opener instance. View

entries.title: Menu.shown
entries.text: Whether the menu is up. Read it; open through openAt/openFor rather than assigning it , or the menu appears unplaced, unraised, and without its keyboard claim. Closing by assignment skips the cascade teardown for the same reason. boolean

entries.title: Menu.hasIcons
entries.text: Whether any row carries an icon — which is what decides the icon gutter exists at all. A menu with no icons has no gutter, and the text edge moves accordingly. boolean

entries.title: Menu.textEdge
entries.text: The x every row's label starts at — one line for the whole menu, icons or not, and what a kind row must align its own content to. number

entries.title: Menu.isRoot
entries.text: False on a cascade child. The root owns the backdrop, the deferred delivery, and the Escape-closes-everything behaviour; a submenu delegates all three upward. boolean

entries.title: Menu.rootMenu
entries.text: The root of this menu's cascade chain — null on the root itself. Menu

entries.title: Menu.child
entries.text: The one lazily-created submenu instance, reused across every row that cascades. A Menu cannot declare a Menu child (it would recurse), so the cascade is built by name at first use. Menu

entries.title: Menu.activeRow
entries.text: The row the keyboard rover currently highlights, or null when the pointer is driving. Read-only in practice. View

entries.title: Menu.picked
entries.text: The delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked row's id, and the id is the whole message. Called after the menu has left the screen, so a slow action can never freeze an open menu. picked(id)

entries.title: Menu.expectedHeight
entries.text: The panel's height before it has been laid out, measured when it exists and estimated from the record count when it does not. The flip-above decision cannot wait for a settle, which is why this exists. expectedHeight()

entries.title: Menu.openAt
entries.text: Opens the menu at the pointer, given the serving view and the pointer event — the context-menu rule. Clamped inside the app like any placement. ContextMenu wraps this as open. openAt(v, e)

entries.title: Menu.openFor
entries.text: Opens the menu anchored below a control, flipping above it when there is not room below and more room above — the native select discipline. The attached-menu rule; what Control.menu uses. openFor(v)

entries.title: Menu.place
entries.text: Positions the panel from root-space coordinates, converting into the parent's space and clamping inside the app — so a menu works declared at App level or inside a component. The chain offset is snapshotted at open: menu chrome does not move while a menu is up. place(x, y)

entries.title: Menu.close
entries.text: Takes the menu down, closes any cascade under it, and releases the keyboard claim. close()

entries.title: Menu.pick
entries.text: Delivers a row: dismisses first, then delivers, one painted frame later — the native menu contract, and the reason a long-running action cannot leave a menu stranded on screen. A submenu routes to the root so the whole chain closes as one. pick(id)

entries.title: Menu.openSub
entries.text: Opens a row's submenu, creating the shared child menu on first use and placing it alongside the row. openSub(row, subItems)

entries.title: Menu.closeSub
entries.text: Closes the cascade under this menu, if any. closeSub()

entries.title: Menu.rootClose
entries.text: Closes the entire chain from wherever it is called — what Escape and an outside press both do. rootClose()

entries.title: Menu.step
entries.text: Moves the keyboard rover by ±1 over the pickable rows, skipping dividers, disabled rows and custom-content rows, and scrolls the landing row into view. step(d)

entries.title: Menu.pickActive
entries.text: Picks the roved row — Enter's action. On a row with a submenu it enters the cascade instead. pickActive()

entries.title: Menu.enterSub
entries.text: Enters the roved row's submenu and puts the rover on its first row — ArrowRight's action. enterSub()

entries.title: MenuBar
entries.text: The record-driven menu bar (planes.md §4–§6): whole menus are DATA — menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] } — and the component arranges. ONE internal Menu serves every title; its items constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state (enabled, checked, labels) stays LIVE while the menu is up. Because the records are the single declaration, an app can derive its key registry from the same array the bar renders — nothing is declared twice (the Newton keys direction, proven in apps/desktop). Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do NOT highlight on mere hover; a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes. Delivery is the one seam: picked(id) — override at the use site. App [ width = 380, height = 120, chose: string = "", bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8, menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }), ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }), ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: MenuBar.menus
entries.text: The whole bar as data: [ { id, label, bold?, kind?, items: [ …menu records… ] } ], where items is exactly Menu's record shape. One internal Menu serves every title , deriving its rows from the open one — so item state stays live while a menu is up, and there is nothing to keep in step. Because the records are the single declaration, an app can derive its keyboard-shortcut registry from the same array the bar renders. array

entries.title: MenuBar.ink
entries.text: Overrides the titles' colour, for a bar drawn straight over a wallpaper where the platform text turns light. null uses the theme's text colour. The dropdown menus stay themed either way — this is the bar's own ink, not the menu's. Color

entries.title: MenuBar.openId
entries.text: Which title's menu is open, by id — "" when none is. string

entries.title: MenuBar.shown
entries.text: Whether any menu in the bar is currently open. boolean

entries.title: MenuBar.picked
entries.text: The delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked item's id from any menu in the bar; the id is the whole message. picked(id)

entries.title: MenuBar.openMenu
