entries.text: Opens a title's menu and keeps the bar itself above the menu's backdrop, which is what lets tracking continue while a menu is up. openMenu(t)

entries.title: MenuBar.trackMenu
entries.text: Switches to another title while a menu is already open — bar tracking: titles do not highlight on mere hover, but once a menu is open, crossing another title opens that one. trackMenu(t)

entries.title: MenuBar.stepMenu
entries.text: Moves to the adjacent title's menu — Left/Right while a menu is open, yielding to the open menu when a submenu is up or the rover sits on one. stepMenu(d)

entries.title: Dialog
entries.text: The modal tier (planes.md): a full-app SCRIM that swallows every press — modal input blocking, no light dismiss — under a centered panel with a focusTrap. Buttons are RECORDS (the records door): { id, label, default?, cancel? }, rendered as themed library Buttons right-aligned in the platform arrangement. Focus SAVES on open and RETURNS on close. Keyboard: Return picks the DEFAULT button (the Cupertino rule; a focused button also activates on Space/Enter — the pick guard makes the double harmless), Escape picks the cancel record when one exists, else just closes. The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id (the picked(id) override remains the declarative seam): dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.") dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …) dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.") ask is Cancel / No / Yes-default; error renders the title in the theme's errorColor. Platform STRUCTURE is data (the scheme): dialogWidth, dialogButtons = "end" (a right-aligned row — SF, Material) "stack" (the stacked alert — full-width buttons stacked, DEFAULT ON TOP) "fill" (WinUI ContentDialog — equal-width buttons filling the row), dialogAlign = "left" "center" (the Cupertino centered title), dialogTitleSize / dialogBodySize. Plus scrimColor + scrimOpacity (Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by SHADOW; Material's spec scrim is 32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the menuShadow family, errorColor. Declare one and call it. A Dialog is not a view you show and hide around your content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves every prompt in the program. App [ width = 340, height = 140, said: string = "", dlg: Dialog [ ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…", onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.", (id) => { app.said = id }) } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ] ]

entries.title: Dialog.shown
entries.text: Whether the dialog is up. Read it; open through a verb (ask, notice, error, open) rather than assigning it, or you get a panel with no buttons, no saved focus, and no focus trap engaged. boolean

entries.title: Dialog.title
entries.text: The heading. Set by the verbs; read it if you are restyling. string

entries.title: Dialog.message
entries.text: The body text under the title. "" hides the line entirely rather than leaving a gap. string

entries.title: Dialog.tone
entries.text: "error" tints the title with the theme's error colour; "" is the ordinary tone. string

entries.title: Dialog.buttons
entries.text: The button records currently rendered, in authored order. The "stack" arrangement reorders them for display — default on top, cancel at the bottom — without touching this. array

entries.title: Dialog.arrangement
entries.text: How the buttons lay out, elected by theme.dialogButtons: "end" (a right-aligned row), "stack" (full-width buttons stacked, Cupertino-style, default on top), or "fill" (equal-width buttons filling the row). Platform structure is data, not a fork. string

entries.title: Dialog.centered
entries.text: Whether the title and message are centre-aligned, elected by theme.dialogAlign. boolean

entries.title: Dialog.picked
entries.text: The declarative delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked button's id. Fires after the dialog has left the screen, and in addition to any callback passed to the verb, so you may use either or both. picked(id)

entries.title: Dialog.open
entries.text: The general form the three idioms are built on: title, message, your own button records, a tone ("error" or ""), and an optional callback. Reach for it when the three idioms do not spell your choices — button records are { id, label, default?, cancel? } , and the two flags are what Return and Escape key off. open(t, m, btns, tone_, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.notice
entries.text: A single-OK acknowledgement. Delivers "ok". notice(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.error
entries.text: A single-OK acknowledgement with the title in the theme's error colour. Delivers "ok". error(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.ask
entries.text: The three-way prompt: Cancel / No / Yes, with Yes as the default. Delivers "cancel", "no" or "yes". ask(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.close
entries.text: Takes the dialog down without delivering anything, and restores focus to whatever held it before. Focus is restored one turn later, deliberately — an immediate restore hands the in-flight keystroke back to the opener, which re-activates and reopens. close()

entries.title: Dialog.pick
entries.text: Delivers a button by id: dismisses first, then delivers, one painted frame later — the same contract as Menu.pick, so a slow action cannot freeze the dialog on screen. Guarded against double activation, so a focused default button answering Space and Return is harmless. pick(id)

entries.title: Dialog.focusDefault
entries.text: Puts keyboard focus on the default button when the dialog opens — or the last button when no record is marked default. focusDefault()

entries.title: Dialog.pickDefault
entries.text: Picks whichever button record carries default: true — Return's action, the Cupertino rule. pickDefault()

entries.title: Dialog.pickCancel
entries.text: Picks the cancel: true record when there is one, else just closes — Escape's action. A dialog with no cancel record still dismisses on Escape, it simply delivers nothing. pickCancel()

entries.title: AppIsland
entries.text: AppIsland embeds a live Declare application: give it a program and it mounts that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view. It composes DOMIsland (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the run:… wire. The page host (browser/host-client.js) sees the key on the box, resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile, identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child. childName (inherited from DOMIsland) is the reverse channel: the running child's appName reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows.

entries.title: AppIsland.program
entries.text: What to run: a program name, a relative path ("../../calendar/calendar" reaches the real app — no copy of the source, ever), or the reserved "raw" live-edit channel, where the running program is the host app's liveSource and recompiles as it changes. "" detaches the island and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a view of itself. string

entries.title: AppIsland.env
entries.text: The embedding environment in query form ("dark=1&base=../x/"), delivered to the child's reactive app.env at mount and on every change. Empty sends none, so the child keeps its own defaults — leave it alone unless the host genuinely overrides something, or you will pin the child's appearance against the system's. string

entries.title: SimpleLayout
entries.text: The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along axis, in child order, spacing apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row with the ordinary y = center. Invisible children are skipped and their space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so re-showing it needs no special case. A Spacer child flexes to absorb the run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run). Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ], View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ], View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ] ]

entries.title: SimpleLayout.axis
entries.text: Which way children stack: y (the default) or x. A bare literal, not a string — axis = x, and note that x here is the axis token, not the position attribute. Axis

entries.title: SimpleLayout.spacing
entries.text: The gap between adjacent children. Negative overlaps them, which is how a stack of cards or avatars is built. number

entries.title: SimpleLayout.place
entries.text: The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order. The cross axis and every size stay the children's own — a child centres itself across a row with the ordinary y = center. Override it in a subclass for custom geometry; a Layout's place() may aggregate over children, which is the one place that is allowed. place()

entries.title: WrappingLayout
entries.text: A horizontal flow that WRAPS: children run left to right spacing apart, and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row (lineSpacing down; -1, the default, means "same as spacing"). With room for one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow on a phone with no media query. It owns BOTH axes of each child (a flow is 2-D); sizes stay the children's own. align justifies each finished row: start (left, the default) or center (a row that does not fill the width sits centered). Division of labor: this is the tool for UNIFORM, replicated collections that reflow by fitting. Managing NAMED regions per width tier is ResponsiveLayout's. Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place(). box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, lineSpacing = 8 ], View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ], View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ], View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ], View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ] ]

entries.title: WrappingLayout.spacing
entries.text: The horizontal gap between children in a row. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.lineSpacing
entries.text: The vertical gap between rows. -1 (the default) means "same as spacing", so a uniform grid needs one number rather than two kept in step. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.align
entries.text: How a finished row is justified: start (the default, left) or center, which centres a row that does not fill the width. A bare literal. WrapAlign

entries.title: WrappingLayout.place
entries.text: Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. It owns both axes of each child — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than looping forever. place()

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout
entries.text: A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows. ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of plans — each one says "from this width up, arrange the children like this" — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes. Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate wiring. bar: View [ layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [ { from: 900, flow: "row", share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } }, { from: 600, flow: "row", share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } }, { from: 0, flow: "stack" }, ] } ], logo: Logo [ ], nav: Nav [ ], actions: Actions [ ], ] Each entry's from means use this plan when the view is at least this wide — the entry with the largest from that fits wins, wherever it sits in the list, and an entry with from: 0 is the fallback for anything narrower. flow is the arrangement: "row" places children left to right; "stack" places them top to bottom. share divides the width (what is left of it after the gaps) among the children it NAMES — the names are the view's own child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is a loud error). logo: 15 gives logo 15% of it; 0 hides that child while the plan is active — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view widens. A child a plan does NOT name is left alone: natural width, the flow just places it. gap sets the space between children (an entry may carry its own gap to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as always. So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split 15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room; below 600, everything stacks. Slack and alignment. When a row's children keep natural widths, the run may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a knob: a Spacer [ ] child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. On the axis the flow does not manage, a child places itself with the ordinary literals (y = center in a row). Shares that fill the width leave no slack at all — shares fill; naturals align. Nesting — who decides what. A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically. Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.) Division of labor. ResponsiveLayout manages NAMED regions. A collection of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool: WrappingLayout (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width constraint on the card. When the rules aren't enough. A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap. Whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a State applied on a width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding place() — the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.plan
entries.text: The storyboard: a list of { from, flow, share?, gap? } entries. from means "use this plan when the view is at least this wide" — the largest from that fits wins, wherever it sits in the list, and from: 0 is the fallback. flow is "row" or "stack". share divides the width among the children it names by their own child names , checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error. A share of 0 hides that child while the plan is active, so "the actions disappear on small screens" is one number, and they return by themselves when the view widens. A child a plan does not name keeps its natural width. array

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.gap
entries.text: The default space between children, overridable per plan entry. number

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.place
entries.text: Selects the active plan from the view's own width — never the window's — and arranges accordingly. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business. place()

entries.title: Spacer
entries.text: When a row (or stack) does not fill its container, the leftover space has to go SOMEWHERE — and the laid children cannot take it themselves (their flow-axis slot is owned by the layout). A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns. Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply zero and invisible in effect. The layout owns a Spacer's flow-axis size (a percent-family constraint, so a container deriving its extent from its children never counts one); the flexes marker is what a flow layout looks for. An empty view otherwise — it paints nothing and has no size of its own.

entries.title: Spacer.flexes
entries.text: The marker a flow layout looks for. True (the default) means the layout owns this Spacer's size along the flow axis and expands it to take up the slack — which is what makes Spacer [ ] push its siblings apart. Set it false for a fixed gap you size yourself. boolean

entries.title: Table
entries.text: The list collection, componentized (docs/system-design/component-briefs.md §2 — D8 RULED): the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or written) collection, carrying the RULED selection model (docs/system-design/selection-model.md) so no app hand-rolls it again: Selection is the Table's VALUE — selected (the primary member) and selection (all of them, presented order), holding MEMBERS: the record for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via input (Contract 1 form b); identity per the ruled ladder (a record's id by convention, else the object itself — the reconciler's own rule). The three facts: selection, the ANCHOR (where ranges extend from), and the keyboard position active — moved by arrows, extended by shift, walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection). selects declares the mode: none single multi (default single). (Build note: the ruled docs used one word for the mode AND the value; the value keeps the ruled name selection, so the mode rides selects.) Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children reaching their table as parent, replicated over data or written by hand. The row template stays free of any selection wiring. Windowing composes: put virtualize on the row template and selection, ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the DATA through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (uniform row extents, the kernel's own v1 assumption). entries.title: Table.selected
entries.text: On a Table, the primary selected member — the record most recently selected, or null. On a TableRow, whether this row's member is in that selection, derived from the table and never stored. Both are members-not-views: selection survives sorts, filters, and windowing because it was never a set of instances. object

entries.title: Table.selection
entries.text: Every selected member, in presented order — null when nothing is selected. Records for a replicated table, the row views themselves for a written one. Never assign it; deliver through input. array

entries.title: Table.active
entries.text: On a Table, the member the keyboard stands on — moved by arrows, and distinct from the selection, which is what makes ⌘-walk-then-Space possible. On a TableRow, whether this row is that one. object

entries.title: Table.selects
entries.text: The mode: "none", "single" (the default), or "multi". Multi is what enables shift-ranges, ⌘-toggles, and the ⌘-walk. string

entries.title: Table.idOf
entries.text: A member's identity: its scalar id field by convention, else the object itself — the same ladder the reconciler uses, so nothing needs declaring for selection to survive a re-sort . idOf(m)

entries.title: Table.same
entries.text: Whether two members are the same one, by idOf. same(a, b)

entries.title: Table.isSelected
entries.text: Whether a member is in the selection, by identity. isSelected(m)

entries.title: Table.isActive
entries.text: Whether a member is the keyboard position, by identity. isActive(m)

entries.title: Table.input
entries.text: Where the selection goes. The default writes selected and selection; override it to own the value (input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel }) and every gesture — click, range, keyboard — routes through your override, because they all land here. input(sel)

entries.title: Table.clearSelection
entries.text: Delivers an empty selection through input. clearSelection()

entries.title: Table.memberAt
entries.text: The member at a logical index. memberAt(i)

entries.title: Table.memberArray
entries.text: The full member universe, read from the data through any row's cursor — never from instances. This is the windowing contract: a table over a virtualized collection can range-select rows that have never been built. memberArray()

entries.title: Table.memberCount
entries.text: How many members there are — the full logical count, not what is materialized. memberCount()

entries.title: Table.rowClick
entries.text: The click protocol: plain click selects exactly one member, ⌘/Ctrl toggles, Shift extends from the anchor. Called by a TableRow; override to change what a click means. rowClick(i, m, toggle, range)

entries.title: Table.step
entries.text: Arrow-key travel: plain moves and selects, Shift extends the range, ⌘ moves the position alone so Space can toggle it. Scrolls the destination into view. step(to, e)

entries.title: Table.showRow
entries.text: Scrolls a row into view by index — using its instance when one exists, and arithmetic when it does not , so arrow travel into unmaterialized rows works and materializes on arrival. showRow(i)

entries.title: Table.deleteRequested
entries.text: Delivery seam — the app declares what deleting is. Fires on Delete or Backspace while there is a selection and the table itself holds focus, so a text field's Backspace is never mistaken for it. Does nothing by default: refusal by inertness. deleteRequested()

entries.title: Table.activateRequested
entries.text: Delivery seam — the app declares what opening is. Fires on Enter on the walked row, under the same focus condition. The list idiom's other half. activateRequested()

entries.title: Table.keyDown
entries.text: Arrows, Home/End, Space (multi), Delete/Backspace and Enter. An override should call through or the table loses its keyboard. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: TableRow
entries.text: The list collection, componentized (docs/system-design/component-briefs.md §2 — D8 RULED): the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or written) collection, carrying the RULED selection model (docs/system-design/selection-model.md) so no app hand-rolls it again: Selection is the Table's VALUE — selected (the primary member) and selection (all of them, presented order), holding MEMBERS: the record for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via input (Contract 1 form b); identity per the ruled ladder (a record's id by convention, else the object itself — the reconciler's own rule). The three facts: selection, the ANCHOR (where ranges extend from), and the keyboard position active — moved by arrows, extended by shift, walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection). selects declares the mode: none single multi (default single). (Build note: the ruled docs used one word for the mode AND the value; the value keeps the ruled name selection, so the mode rides selects.) Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children reaching their table as parent, replicated over data or written by hand. The row template stays free of any selection wiring. Windowing composes: put virtualize on the row template and selection, ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the DATA through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (uniform row extents, the kernel's own v1 assumption). []).length + " selected" } ] ]

entries.title: TableRow.selected
entries.text: On a Table, the primary selected member — the record most recently selected, or null. On a TableRow, whether this row's member is in that selection, derived from the table and never stored. Both are members-not-views: selection survives sorts, filters, and windowing because it was never a set of instances. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.active
entries.text: On a Table, the member the keyboard stands on — moved by arrows, and distinct from the selection, which is what makes ⌘-walk-then-Space possible. On a TableRow, whether this row is that one. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.member
entries.text: The member this row presents: its record when replicated, the row view itself when written by hand. member()

entries.title: TableRow.rowIndex
entries.text: This row's logical index in data order — read from the cursor when replicated, so it is true under windowing. A method rather than a slot because its consumers are gestures, and the written-row fallback walks children, which no constraint may do. rowIndex()

entries.title: TableRow.pointerDown
entries.text: Focuses the table, not the row — rows are never tab stops, so the arrow keys must land on the container. onPointerDown()

entries.title: TableRow.click
entries.text: Delivers the click to the table's rowClick with the modifier state. Override rowClick on the table rather than this, unless a particular row needs to opt out. onClick()

entries.title: Combobox
entries.text: Filter-as-you-type over a collection (component-briefs.md §3 — D8 RULED): a text field owning a QUERY plus a dismissable option list owning a CHOICE — the canonical derived selection over data. Composition, not invention: TextInput for the entry, the Menu machinery for the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss, Escape closes — the whole dismissal discipline rides along), and the matches are a DERIVED collection — a constraint over the items array, so the live match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned. Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee", items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ] Items are members (the selection model's currency): records — shown by their label (or id) — or plain strings. value holds the CHOSEN member; input(v) is the delivery seam (Contract 1): the default writes value, a use-site override redirects and the slot stays untouched. Typing filters live (case-insensitive substring); opening WITHOUT typing shows the full list (the disclosure-button read). Picking echoes the label into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text. Keyboard: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved row — or the FIRST match when none is roved (the type-then-Enter path); Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own. The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and virtualize applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes). App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "", people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] }, Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee", items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ] ]

entries.title: Combobox.items
entries.text: The options, as members: records — shown by their label, else id — or plain strings. The currency of the selection model, so whatever you put in is what comes back out of input. array

entries.title: Combobox.value
entries.text: The chosen member, not the typed text — the whole record when you supplied records. null until something is picked. Standalone the combobox owns it; bound, override input beside it. object

entries.title: Combobox.placeholder
entries.text: The entry's placeholder text while empty. string

entries.title: Combobox.query
entries.text: What the user has typed since the last pick. Not the value — the draft that filters the list. string

entries.title: Combobox.filtering
entries.text: Whether the user has typed since the last pick. False means a bare disclosure, which shows the whole list rather than filtering against a stale query — the difference between clicking the chevron and typing. boolean

entries.title: Combobox.matches
entries.text: The filtered options, as a derived collection: a constraint over items, so the live match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned. Case-insensitive substring against each member's label. array

entries.title: Combobox.matchCount
entries.text: How many options currently match — read it straight, rather than counting list rows, which is both wrong under virtualization and refused by the compiler. number

entries.title: Combobox.list
entries.text: The option list — a Menu created at the app layer on first open, not a child of the combobox, so it paints over everything rather than only over later siblings. All the overlay behaviour arrives with it: light dismiss, Escape, the arrow rover, the viewport flip, the long-list scroll. View

entries.title: Combobox.labelOf
entries.text: How a member is displayed: a record's label, else its id, else the value itself. Override to display members your own way. labelOf(m)

entries.title: Combobox.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes. Receives the chosen member. The default writes value; an override redirects it and leaves the slot untouched. input(v)

entries.title: Combobox.pickIndex
entries.text: Picks the nth current match: echoes its label into the entry, closes the list, and delivers the member through input. The index is into matches, never into items. pickIndex(i)

entries.title: Combobox.ensureList
entries.text: Creates the shared list on first use and wires its delivery back to pickIndex. ensureList()

entries.title: Combobox.syncList
entries.text: Pushes the current matches into the list — called on every keystroke. syncList()

entries.title: Combobox.closeList
entries.text: Closes the list without picking. closeList()

entries.title: Combobox.listShown
entries.text: Whether the list is currently up. listShown()

entries.title: Combobox.listRoved
entries.text: Whether the keyboard rover is sitting on a row. This is what makes Enter mean two things : pick the roved row when there is one, else take the first match — the type-then-Enter path. listRoved()

entries.title: Combobox.open
entries.text: Opens the full list unfiltered — the disclosure-button path. open()

entries.title: Combobox.toggle
entries.text: Opens the list, or closes it if it is already open. toggle()

entries.title: ContextMenu
entries.text: The right-click / long-press menu (component-briefs.md §4 — D8 RULED): Menu's machinery WHOLE — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (outside press closes AND is swallowed), Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. No new overlay machinery, by the brief's own constraint: if ContextMenu ever needs something Menu lacks, Menu grows it and both ride. Declared ONCE, opened by many. The SERVING view declares the gesture — that declaration is what routes it (the claim model: contextMenu engages the right-click/two-finger path, hold is the touch long-press gate, and each engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on the view the menu serves: rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ], … Row [ …, onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ] open(v, e) anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener (items = { … opener … } for per-row menus with zero per-row instances); picking delivers through picked(id) and closes. Everything else — items, opener, picked, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is Menu's, documented there. App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "", rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }), ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray, onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: ContextMenu.open
entries.text: Opens the menu anchored at the pointer, given the serving view and the pointer event — Menu.openAt under the name the two-line wiring reads best with. The serving view declares the gesture, and that declaration is what routes it : onContextMenu engages the right-click and two-finger path, onHold the touch long-press. Neither engages anywhere a handler is not declared, so a context menu costs nothing on views that do not offer one. open(v, e)

entries.title: DataGrid
entries.text: The Table contract plus a COLUMN MODEL (component-briefs.md §5 — D8 RULED): headers, sortable, reorderable and resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a windowed collection — the header drags are the forcing case the axis-scoped claim = x was designed for. DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value }, selects = "multi", Column [ title = "ID", field = "id", width = 70 ], Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ], Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ] Columns are written members (Column — selection-model §1b: permanent, authored, identity = the child): title heads the column, field names what a cell shows, width is the authored width — a PLAIN value (the column model derives through an unanalyzed children walk; a responsive width belongs in the grid's widths state, which IS a tracked dep: widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }). A column's id is its field (title as fallback). Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state (Contract 1 form b): order (column ids, presented order) and widths (id → width overrides). Reorder delivers through arrangeInput(order), resize through resizeInput(id, w) — defaults write the slots; an app override owns them (persisted layouts). Widths are PLAIN VALUES — nothing measures cells. Header interactions: click sorts — a DELIVERY (sortInput(on, dir) writing sortOn/sortDir by default): sort NAMES a derivation, the truth stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the order its collection has). Horizontal drag REORDERS (live swap at the midpoint); the right-edge grip RESIZES. Both drags declare claim = x — on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x. Rows: the use site writes ONE bare GridRow template over its rows path — cells generate from the column model, each showing record[field]. Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — virtualize on the template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets the window's geometry (the kernel's leading anchor). Focus: land-as-one-stop, browse mode (arrows navigate rows). Entry-mode grids (focusScope = capture, the tax-form convention) are a later increment; nothing here forecloses it. AT: rows speak logical position (the Surface seam). The column dimension (aria-colcount/colindex) is DEFERRED to the same seam — noted, not wired, in v1. Narrow widths: v1 clips (clip on the cell); the deliberate degrade (priority, not squish) is a designed later increment per the brief. Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are Table's, documented there. What follows is only the column model. App [ width = 440, height = 220, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail", "state": "open" }, { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" }, { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid", "state": "open" } ] } }, DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value }, selects = "multi", Column [ title = "ID", field = "id", width = 50 ], Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ], Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ] ] ] Drag a header sideways to reorder; drag the divider between two headers to resize; click a header to sort.

entries.title: DataGrid.headerH
entries.text: The header row's height. number

entries.title: DataGrid.order
entries.text: The presented column order, as column ids — null means authored order. Part of the grid's value-pattern state: delivered through arrangeInput, so an app that overrides that owns the order and can persist it. array

entries.title: DataGrid.widths
entries.text: Per-column width overrides, { id: width } — null means authored widths. A width of 0 drops the column entirely , which is the deliberate narrow-screen degrade: priority, not squish. widths = { app.narrow ? ({ notes: 0 }) : null } is a responsive layout. object

entries.title: DataGrid.sortOn
entries.text: The column id the sort names — "" when unsorted. Sorting names a derivation; it does not reorder anything. The truth stays in the data: your app derives the sorted dataset from this, and the grid displays the order its collection already has. string

entries.title: DataGrid.sortDir
entries.text: "asc" or "desc", alongside sortOn. string

entries.title: DataGrid.colVersion
entries.text: Bump this to rebuild the column model when columns are added or removed at runtime. The model derives through a children walk, which no constraint can track — so this is the manual nudge that stands in for one. number

entries.title: DataGrid.escaped
entries.text: Whether the header surface has left the grid's scrolling box for its parent. The grid's box is the rows' scroll region exactly — the scrollbar spans rows only, and no row ever slides under the header. Backends without the ride keep an in-box header. boolean

entries.title: DataGrid.sortInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for sorting. The default writes sortOn/sortDir; override it to own the sort — which is what you do when the sorted collection is derived app-side, or when the sort belongs to a server query. sortInput(on, dir)

entries.title: DataGrid.arrangeInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for reordering, receiving the new column-id order. Override it to persist a user's column layout. arrangeInput(ord)

entries.title: DataGrid.resizeInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for resizing, receiving a column id and its new width. Widths are plain values — nothing measures cells — so an override is free to clamp, snap, or store them. resizeInput(id, w)

entries.title: DataGrid.headerClick
entries.text: Toggles the sort on a column: same column flips direction, a new column starts ascending. Routes through sortInput. headerClick(id)

entries.title: DataGrid.columnRecords
entries.text: The derived column model — the authored Column children, ordered and widthed by state, with running x offsets. The one truth every header cell and grid cell positions from. State arrives as arguments precisely so the deriving constraint tracks it. columnRecords(v, ord, w)

entries.title: DataGrid.colId
entries.text: A column's id: its field, falling back to its title. colId(c)

entries.title: DataGrid.currentOrder
entries.text: The column ids in their present order. currentOrder()

entries.title: DataGrid.editStep
entries.text: Moves an active "edit" cell's focus one row up or down in the same column — the spreadsheet expectation. Scrolls the destination into existence first, so it works over a windowed collection. editStep(row, field, d)

entries.title: DataGrid.colWidthOf
entries.text: The present width of a column by id. colWidthOf(id)

entries.title: DataGrid.openSelect
entries.text: Opens the shared options menu for a "select" cell and writes the picked value into the record through the row's cursor. One menu serves every select cell in the grid. openSelect(row, cell, field, current)

entries.title: DataGrid.init
entries.text: Requests the header's escape from the scroll box (see escaped). The request stands: the runtime applies it when the view attaches, so init running before attach costs nothing. onInit()

Narrow widths: v1 clips (clip on the cell); the deliberate degrade (priority, not squish) is a designed later increment per the brief. Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are Table's, documented there. What follows is only the column model. App [ width = 440, height = 220, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail", "state": "open" }, { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" }, { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid", "state": "open" } ] } }, DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value }, selects = "multi", Column [ title = "ID", field = "id", width = 50 ], Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ], Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ] ] ] Drag a header sideways to reorder; drag the divider between two headers to resize; click a header to sort.

entries.title: GridRow.rec
entries.text: The row's record, as a derived slot. A slot rather than a method call, so cells re-derive when the record's fields change — a method read would go stale. null on a written (unreplicated) row. object

entries.title: Segmented
entries.text: A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are data, like Menu's items and DataGrid's columns: Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }), ({ id: "table", label: "Table" }), ({ id: "grid", label: "DataGrid" }) ] }, input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v } ] Why data, and not Segment children Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask the view tree that: childViews carries set membership only, so .length is live while anything reaching into the collection is refused — aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]. The compiler names the answer. It is also the mainstream shape. Most native toolkits take segments as titles in an array, picks from a ForEach, Ant Design takes options; only Material and WinUI name the item at all, and both compound it. A bare Segment class was the minority pattern — and bare enough that two apps in this corpus had taken the name for a paragraph of prose. Equal widths — a choice, not a limitation Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a DESIGN decision and it could be otherwise: a Layout's place() may aggregate over children — that is how SimpleLayout sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is buildable. The DECLARE7001 refusal binds constraints reaching into the view tree, not the layout strategy whose job that is. Three reasons not to: The systems that call this a segmented control agree. The native ones divide evenly by default, as does the classic segmented Picker. The ones that size to content — Bootstrap, Ant — are really styling a row of buttons. The segmented convention makes it a content rule: keep segment labels short and similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want. The sliding pill. At equal widths it translates at constant width. At variable widths it would have to morph its width WHILE travelling, which reads as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet this, because their highlight pops. The cost is real and worth stating plainly: a Segmented does not self-size to its labels. Set width, or accept segMin × choices.length. The pill The highlight springs a NORMALIZED LANE — a float index — not pixels. x is then lane × segW, so a resize recomputes segW and the pill snaps to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. Calendar's tab strip discovered this; it is the one thing the bespoke copies did better than the library, and it is now here. The look is the library's: the chosen segment wears a raised surface pill with a hairline. The motion is calendar's. Neither app was wrong about the half it got right (chrome-divergences.md D9). App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one", Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }), ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }), ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] }, input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ] ]

entries.title: Segmented.choices
entries.text: The segments, as records: { id, label } or { id, icon } — the same vocabulary Menu's items use. A choice shows a label or an icon, never both. A choice may also carry a location, which makes that segment a real link (see SegmentedItem.location). array

entries.title: Segmented.value
entries.text: The active choice. Bind it to your own state and override input to own the destination, or leave it alone and read value back — a Segmented works standalone. Compared against each item's choice by identity, so any value type works. object

entries.title: Segmented.disabled
entries.text: Disables the whole control. A segment is not separately disable-able — a disabled group leaves the tab order entirely rather than offering unreachable stops. boolean

entries.title: Segmented.segMin
entries.text: The per-segment width used when you set no width on the control. Because a Segmented does not self-size to its labels, this is what decides the default width: segMin × choices.length. number

entries.title: Segmented.count
entries.text: How many choices there are, floored at 1 so the width arithmetic never divides by zero. number

entries.title: Segmented.segW
entries.text: One segment's width — the control's width divided by the count. What the pill and every segment position from. number

entries.title: Segmented.idx
entries.text: Which choice is live, as an index into choices, from the data — the only place the question can be asked. −1 (nothing selected) parks the pill at 0 and hides it rather than springing to a phantom slot. number

entries.title: Segmented.lane
entries.text: The pill's position as a float index, sprung toward idx. The whole reason the pill is correct at any size: x is lane × segW, so a resize recomputes the width and the pill snaps to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. number

entries.title: Segmented.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes, receiving the picked id. The default writes value; override it to own the destination. input(v)

entries.title: Segmented.pick
entries.text: Selects a choice by id, routing through input. The seam a segment calls. pick(v)

entries.title: Segmented.segs
entries.text: The segment views, for the keyboard rove. A handler-only walk — a constraint may not aggregate the view tree. segs()

entries.title: Segmented.roveFrom
entries.text: Moves keyboard focus to the adjacent segment. Arrows rove; Space or Enter picks where they land, so an inactive choice is reachable and selectable entirely from the keyboard . roveFrom(seg, d)

entries.title: ChevronIcon
entries.text: The disclosure mark: a menu drops, a pane opens, a select expands. Every disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its dir, which is what makes them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach for ArrowIcon instead; the two must not look alike.

entries.title: ChevronIcon.dir
entries.text: The resting orientation: "down" (the default), "up", "left" or "right". Sugar over angle. string

entries.title: ChevronIcon.angle
entries.text: The rotation in radians, and the primitive, so it can be sprung — an Accordion twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its 16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level rotation attribute turns the whole box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.) number

entries.title: ChevronIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the chevron. Override to replace the mark while keeping the class's role. draw(d)

entries.title: CheckIcon
entries.text: The tick — a checked menu row, a Checkbox's mark, a confirmation. Ink stays local : a menu row inverts its check on the highlighted row while a checkbox always uses the accent text colour, so the host sets ink rather than the icon assuming it.

entries.title: CheckIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the tick. Before this class the corpus drew a checkmark two ways — stroke 2.5 mitered in Checkbox, 1.8 round in Menu — which is the drift one shape ends. draw(d)

entries.title: CloseIcon
entries.text: The dismiss mark: a window close box, a chip's remove affordance, a dialog's corner.

entries.title: CloseIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the cross. draw(d)

entries.title: PlusIcon
entries.text: Add. Pairs with MinusIcon at the same stroke and cap, so a stepper's two ends match.

entries.title: PlusIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the plus. draw(d)

entries.title: MinusIcon
entries.text: Remove, and the partially-checked state of a tri-state box. Pairs with PlusIcon.

entries.title: MinusIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the bar. draw(d)

entries.title: LightbulbIcon
entries.text: The help affordance — the one FILLED mark in a stroked set: a continuous teardrop of glass over a three-bar tapering base.

entries.title: LightbulbIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the bulb. This one mark is filled, and does not answer to weight — the contour carries its weight in the outline itself, so there is no stroke to widen. The bulb keeps its own visual weight at every rung. draw(d)

entries.title: SunIcon
entries.text: "Light" in the appearance triad — a disc with rays, sharing its radius and stroke with MoonIcon and AutoIcon so the three read as one family at 14px, which three font glyphs never did.

entries.title: SunIcon.rays
entries.text: How many rays surround the disc. Eight by default; lowering it reads lighter at small sizes. number

entries.title: SunIcon.solid
entries.text: false (the default) draws the ring; true fills the disc. The ring is drawn a touch smaller than the filled disc on purpose — a stroke straddles its path, so an outline at the filled radius reads as the larger mark. boolean

entries.title: SunIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the disc and its rays. draw(d)

entries.title: MoonIcon
entries.text: "Dark" in the appearance triad. The crescent is the region between two equal circles , the second offset by (3, −3) — so both arcs meet exactly at the circles' intersection points and the horns close to a point instead of leaving the ragged tail an arc pair leaves.

entries.title: MoonIcon.solid
entries.text: false (the default) strokes the closed path — the tapered-horn rendition; true fills it for a solid crescent. One path, two renditions — nothing about the geometry changes, only what is done with it. boolean

entries.title: MoonIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the crescent. draw(d)

entries.title: AutoIcon
entries.text: "System" in the appearance triad — the same disc, half of it taken away. The ring stays around the empty half so it reads as part of one object rather than as a gap. The one mark of the three whose meaning is its fill, which is why a mixed outline-and-filled language is right for the triad.

entries.title: AutoIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the half-filled disc. draw(d)

entries.title: Icon
entries.text: A small monochrome mark, drawn rather than typed. Fonts are not UI objects: their glyphs are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a ✓ sits on the text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The house already knew this in three places before it had a name for it (Checkbox.mark, Menu.check, Combobox.disc are all drawn); this is that decision, stated once. Writing one Subclass and override draw. Author the shape in a 16×16 box — unit converts it to whatever size the host asked for: class SparkIcon extends Icon [ draw(d: Draw) { d.scale(unit, unit) d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke() } ] Overriding a method is the refinement path that works — re-opening an inherited child is not (cap: on a Button subclass fails at instantiate), so the shape lives in draw and everything adjustable is a slot. Size changes the drawing, not the shape Every icon is ONE path. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing redrawn at a breakpoint: unit scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for, so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly. The stroke is the deliberate exception. d.lineWidth = weight / unit sits inside d.scale(unit, unit), so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant weight in device pixels at every size. An icon's line therefore matches the 1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows. The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5% at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px, which is every site in this corpus, that is invisible. Past ~32 an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so this set is built for chrome sizes, and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an about-box graphic) would want the opposite: d.lineWidth = weight outside the scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon systems take a third road and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger undertaking than this set needs. test/probe/iconbook.declare shows the ramp — the same chevron and bulb at 16, 24, 32, 48 and 64 — if the tradeoff ever needs re-judging. What is NOT an Icon Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification swell, they are polychrome (gradient(hue1, hue2) behind a hue-parameterised drawing), and their width animates every frame. Each of those alone rules them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and reads spindly; ink is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing this set forbids. The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is chrome vocabulary versus identity. A mark that says close, expand, checked, this is the dark theme belongs here, at a size the host states. A mark that says this is Calendar does not, and belongs to the app that owns the identity. Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows take WindowIcon and CodeIcon from this set, while its dock keeps DockIcon. Two rules Scale inside the body, never with the View's scale. A recording rasterizes into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution (dom-backend.ts rasterize()), while scale is a CSS transform applied after — so scale = { width / 16 } would rasterize 16 pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size instead. Never animate an icon's width. Reading size inside draw makes the recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records AND reallocates the backing canvas every frame, which is what dragged the dock's magnification from 60 to ~25fps (adaptive-draw-cache.md). A static size re-records once and costs nothing after. Measured: 120 icons re-recording their content every frame runs frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper than the 120 text glyphs they replace. Colour is not a rule — ink follows the prevailing text colour, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

entries.title: Icon.ink
entries.text: The mark's colour. Follows the prevailing textColor, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own. The trap: that slot falls back to black platform-wide, so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a dark surface. State ink unless you know the context sets one — IconHost does it for every icon built by name. Color

entries.title: Icon.weight
entries.text: Stroke width in final device pixels, not authored ones. Divide by unit inside draw (d.lineWidth = weight / unit) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among. number

entries.title: Icon.unit
entries.text: The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by it. Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants. number

entries.title: IconHost
entries.text: A control names its icon (iconLeft = TrashIcon) rather than nesting one, because a control is a leaf and everything else about it is an attribute — and because an attribute is the one form where AUTHORED and BOUND are the same mechanism. IconHost is what turns that name into a live view, through the same app.createView seam the menu's iconKind already uses. It reserves no space when empty, so a control's contentWidth measures only the slots that are actually filled and an icon-less button needs no special case. LIMITATION, deliberate for now: the name is consumed once, at construction. A control whose icon must CHANGE at runtime (a play/pause toggle) is not served by this yet — that needs a name-valued slot the runtime re-materializes on change, which is a runtime feature, not a library one. Every site in this corpus names its icon statically.

entries.title: IconHost.kind
entries.text: The icon class name to build ("TrashIcon"). "" builds nothing and the host collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. Consumed once, at construction — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name that is only ever computed needs use [ Name ] to survive the build. string

entries.title: IconHost.ink
entries.text: The colour handed to the icon this host builds. createView cannot pass attributes, so a prevailing slot is the only channel that reaches it — this publishes textColor for exactly that. Defaults to theme.text rather than the platform's inherited black, which is what stops a host-built icon from rendering invisibly on a dark surface. Color

entries.title: IconHost.init
entries.text: Builds the named icon. Fires once. onInit()

entries.title: SegmentedItem
entries.text: One choice of a Segmented, materialized from that control's choices data — never authored directly , which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full Control: its own tab stop, activated by Space or Enter, so a user can tab to an inactive choice and select it. It renders rest, hover and press only. The chosen state is the sliding pill behind these, not a fill of its own — which is exactly what lets the pill travel between segments instead of popping.

entries.title: SegmentedItem.on
entries.text: Whether this segment is the group's current choice, derived from the parent by identity. boolean

entries.title: SegmentedItem.ink
entries.text: This segment's text and icon colour, brightening when it is on or hot. One slot, so a label and an icon can never disagree. Color

entries.title: SegmentedItem.location
entries.text: Makes this segment a real link: give a choice a location and the segment navigates there in its own onClick. This is what keeps a view-switching control visible to link extraction — the crawler reads app.location = … out of activation handlers, and input(v) is not one, since its destination depends on a value that does not exist at extraction time. Empty for an ordinary segmented control, and an empty read emits no anchor. string

entries.title: SegmentedItem.press
entries.text: Delivers this segment's id to the group. press()

entries.title: SegmentedItem.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the segment's pill inset, not its whole box. focusShape()

entries.title: SegmentedItem.click
entries.text: Navigates if the choice carries a location, then presses. onClick()

entries.title: SegmentedItem.keyDown
entries.text: Space and Enter pick; arrows rove to the adjacent segment. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: ArrowIcon
entries.text: An arrow, not a chevron — the two mean different things and must not look alike. A chevron discloses; an arrow points at a direction that is itself the state: sort ascending, a trend, a transfer. The shaft is what a chevron lacks. Tracker had the two adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape for both read as a mistake.

entries.title: ArrowIcon.dir
entries.text: Which way it points: "up" (the default), "down", "left" or "right". string

entries.title: ArrowIcon.angle
entries.text: The rotation in radians, sprungable like ChevronIcon's. number

entries.title: ArrowIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the arrow. draw(d)
